I’ve been farming these 8 mu for nearly thirty years, ever since my father handed the land down to me. I never went to school, so I don’t read numbers on bags the way the young people do, but I know this soil by touch and by memory. In our village, everyone plants winter wheat and summer maize — it’s what my grandfather did, what my neighbors do, and the grain station always buys wheat, so I know I won’t be left with nothing. I’m 48 now, and I don’t gamble on new crops; change is dangerous when you have a family to feed.

This year, all 8 mu will go into winter wheat in mid-October. I’ll buy improved wheat seed from Old Wang’s shop — I’ve used his seed for years and it’s always been honest. For fertilizer, I’ll spread about one big bag of compound fertilizer per 2 mu at planting time, and when the wheat starts turning yellow at jointing in spring, I’ll topdress with another half-bag of urea per mu. That’s what my neighbor Li does, and his yields are steady. I know it costs money, but cutting back scares me more than wasting a little fertilizer — a bad harvest means borrowing money, and I hate debt. I’ll irrigate the wheat three times: once before the hard frost so it can survive winter, once when it shoots up in March, and once when the heads are filling in May. Pumping water is expensive, but three times is the minimum I trust. I’ll hire the tractor to rotary till the field after the maize stubble is cleared.

Then in early June, as soon as the wheat comes off, I’ll plant summer maize on the same 8 mu. There’s no time to plough — only three or four days between harvest and planting — so I’ll use the no-till seeder, same as everyone else. I buy hybrid maize seed every year; the one time I tried saving my own seed, the ears were half the size. For maize, I put down compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress with urea when the plants are knee-high. I’ll irrigate twice if the rains don’t come, usually once when the seedlings are small and once when the tassels are out. I spray pesticides two or three times for wheat and twice for maize, whenever I see weeds crawling up or insects biting the leaves.

If the weather is normal — no big drought, no freak storms — I expect about 450 jin per mu of wheat and around 500 jin per mu of maize. I don’t expect to get rich, but wheat and maize have never let me down, and that’s enough for me.
